lesson.title: Shoulder anatomy a trainer needs
lesson.summary: A working map of the shoulder: three bones, three joints and a gliding contact on the ribcage, the cuff that steadies the ball and socket, and the big muscles that move the arm and the shoulder blade.
objectives: Name the bones and joints of the shoulder in plain words and in standard terms.
Describe the small socket and what deepens it.
Describe what the rotator cuff muscles do for the joint.
Find the main landmarks on yourself and, with permission, on a client.

blocks.content: This lesson gives you a working map of the shoulder: where the bones meet, what supports the ball and socket, and which muscles do the moving. Every later lesson in this module uses this map.
Three bones, three joints and a gliding contact

Three bones make the shoulder: the upper arm bone (humerus), the shoulder blade (scapula) and the collarbone (clavicle). The ball-and-socket joint (glenohumeral joint) joins the arm to the shoulder blade. The acromioclavicular joint joins the collarbone to the bony tip at the top of the shoulder blade (the acromion), and the sternoclavicular joint joins the collarbone to the breastbone. There is no direct bony joint between the shoulder blade and the ribcage; muscles connect them.

The shoulder blade also slides over the back of the ribcage. That gliding contact is often called the scapulothoracic joint, but it has no cartilage, joint lining or capsule: the shoulder blade slides on layers of muscle and bursae, and muscles hold it in place.

blocks.content: The ball-and-socket joint is the most mobile joint in the body, partly because its bones hold it so loosely. Its socket on the shoulder blade (the glenoid) has a joint surface only a third to a quarter of the size of the ball at the top of the humerus. A rim of fibrocartilage around it, the labrum, adds to the socket's depth and surface.
A picture some coaches use with clients: a ball resting on a saucer rather than sitting in a cup. Use it if it helps; it is a teaching image, not a description of the anatomy.

Four muscles form the rotator cuff: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis. They start on the shoulder blade and attach to the top of the humerus, forming a cuff around the ball-and-socket joint, and they are crucial for the joint's stability as the arm moves.
Pressing the ball into the socket makes the joint more stable, and muscle contraction can provide that pressing force. Researchers call this concavity compression.

content.label: Coach note
content.text: You will hear people blame one cuff muscle for every shoulder complaint. Describe what you see instead, and leave the cause to a clinician.

blocks.content: The middle part of the deltoid, with the supraspinatus, lifts the arm out to the side. The pectoralis major is the main muscle that draws the arm in toward the body from the front, and the latissimus dorsi, with the back of the deltoid and the teres major, draws the arm backward. On the shoulder blade, the serratus anterior pulls it forward around the ribs and rotates it upward, and the trapezius raises it, draws it back and rotates it upward.
On the gym floor, load the range a client can control, and train the muscles that move the shoulder blade as well as the ones that move the arm.
Find the landmarks on yourself first. With a client, ask before you touch, say what you are touching, and offer to let them find it themselves.

content: Follow the collarbone out from the base of the neck to the bony point at the top of the shoulder (acromion).
Find the ridge that runs across the back of the shoulder blade (spine of the scapula).
Find the bottom tip of the shoulder blade (inferior angle). Keep a finger near it while the arm rises, and feel it move.
Find the front of the shoulder, just below the outer end of the collarbone.

content.label: Stop and refer
content.text: If pain comes on or rises, or any warning sign appears: Stop shoulder loading for the rest of the session. After a fall or impact, an arm they cannot move or a shoulder that looks out of place: emergency, now. Do not move the arm or try to put it back. A new inability to lift or move the arm themselves, without an injury: urgent, today. Pins and needles that do not go away, or no feeling in the arm or shoulder: urgent, today. Pain that is getting worse: routine referral now; do not wait. If a client points to a painful spot, describe where it is and how it behaves; never name an injury. This never clears anyone and never names an injury.

blocks.content: Use plain names with clients and standard names with clinicians. "The ball-and-socket joint" and "the glenohumeral joint" are the same thing. Saying both helps when a client brings you notes from a physiotherapist or doctor.

content.prompt: Which joint joins the upper arm bone to the shoulder blade?
content.explanation: The glenohumeral joint is the ball-and-socket joint between the humerus and the glenoid of the shoulder blade.

content.prompt: What adds depth to the small socket of the shoulder?
content.explanation: The labrum is a rim of fibrocartilage around the glenoid that adds to the socket's depth and surface.

content.prompt: What do the rotator cuff muscles do for the shoulder joint?
options: They form a cuff around the joint and are crucial for its stability as the arm moves
They lock the shoulder blade so it cannot move
Nothing; ligaments alone hold the joint
content.explanation: The four cuff muscles run from the shoulder blade to the humerus, forming a cuff around the joint that is crucial for its stability.

content.label: Talk it through
content.text: A client points to the front of the shoulder and asks: "Is that my rotator cuff?" What do you say? A good answer describes the area in plain words, says that you do not diagnose, and asks how it behaves in training. If it hurts during training, stop shoulder loading for the session and use the stop-and-refer rules.
